paras: The Thomasville posse hunt for Manuel Harty was an armed manhunt near Thomasville, Georgia, in August 1905, in which mounted townsmen followed the sheriff in pursuit of a Black farmhand accused of assaulting a farmer's wife and threatened to lynch him if they caught him. Harty was not reported captured; the posse brought in another Black man, who was released when the woman did not identify him. White papers in Georgia and Florida carried the story under headlines predicting a lynching.

According to a Thomasville dispatch of August 17, Harty was a Thomasville man who had worked only two days for Chas. Outze, a young farmer living three miles south of town. The dispatch said that at about 7 a.m., while Outze was boiling syrup half a mile away, Harty came to the house asking for the key to the cotton house, seized and choked Mrs. Outze, and assaulted her before fleeing through the woods with a pistol and a shotgun from the kitchen. The Associated Press version stated that Harty "criminally assaulted" her and added that she was "not fatally injured" and was expecting a child.

Outze rode to Thomasville for a doctor and the officers, and Sheriff T. J. Hight and three deputies left at 8:30 a.m. Within minutes they were followed by "a squad of armed men on horseback, threatening lynching if the negro should fall into their hands." Men gathered at the Confederate monument on Broad Street to plan the pursuit, "every saddle horse in Thomasville was pressed into service," and the roads filled with horses and vehicles carrying armed men to the farm. By late afternoon Harty had not been found, and the Associated Press reported that his capture was expected to "be followed by violence."

On the morning of August 18 the posse returned with a Black man it suspected of the assault and took him to Mrs. Outze to be identified. Being "the wrong man," he was released. The hunt went on: the Madison, Florida, New Enterprise reported that five Thomasville citizens, J. J. Stephens, M. R. Elder, G. M. Powell, Geo. Dopson and W. W. Linton, reached Madison the previous Saturday pursuing a Black man wanted for an "attempted outrage" near Thomasville, after a report that he had been seen in the north of the county.
The Madison paper said the man was not captured, and no later report of Harty's arrest, trial or death appears in the coverage.

The fullest account, printed on the front page of the Americus Times-Recorder on August 18, ran under the headlines "Woman Assaulted by Black Brute," "Georgia Mob Hunting for Perpetrator of Crime" and "Lynching Is Very Probable," and called Harty a "negro fiend." It presented the accusation as fact, described the "whole community" as "aroused over the awful crime," and reported the lynching threat without criticism. The Gainesville Daily Sun reprinted the same dispatch twice in its August 19 issue, in garbled form and with the dateline misprinted as August 15.

The Pensacola Journal carried shorter Associated Press items on August 18 and 19, the second under the headline "Posse Got Wrong Man," which recorded the release without comment on the detention. The Madison New Enterprise mentioned the posse in its local column, calling the men "vigilant in the pursuit." All of these accounts appeared in white papers; no report of the manhunt was found in the Black press, including the Atlanta Independent's Thomasville column.

The Thomasville and Associated Press dispatches, written on the day of the alleged attack, described a completed assault, while the Madison item a week later called it an "attempted outrage." Both versions rest on the accusation against Harty, and no account from him or any hearing appears in the coverage.

bases: Armed horsemen pursued the accused man while threatening to lynch him and a posse detained and released another man, but no one is reported killed or injured by the pursuers (A1, A2, A6, A7).

accounts.label: Thomasville dispatch
accounts.gist: Harty assaulted and choked Mrs. Outze and fled with stolen guns; the sheriff and deputies were followed by armed horsemen threatening lynching, and a lynching was called 'very probable'.

accounts.label: Associated Press
accounts.gist: A posse was searching for Harty, who had not been found by late afternoon; violence was expected on capture; next day the posse brought in the wrong man, who was released.

accounts.label: Madison, Fla. local item
accounts.gist: Five named Thomasville citizens pursued a Black man wanted for an 'attempted outrage' into Madison County; he was not captured.

framing.detail: The Thomasville dispatch ran under 'Woman Assaulted by Black Brute' and 'Lynching Is Very Probable', called the accused a 'negro fiend' and described a 'whole community' 'aroused over the awful crime' without criticism of the lynching threat.
The Associated Press items in the Pensacola Journal stated the charge as fact and predicted violence in a flat tone ('Negro Assaults Farmer's Wife', 'Posse Got Wrong Man').
The Madison New Enterprise reported the posse's visit in its local column, calling the men 'vigilant in the pursuit'.

conflicts.note: The Thomasville and AP dispatches, written the day of the event, state a completed assault; the Madison item a week later calls it attempted. Both are unsworn accounts of an accusation.
The Gainesville reprints misprint the dateline of the same dispatch; August 17 is the original.
